title: Spot the broken min
idea: TOOL: recognise min mistakes — wrong comparison (forgot to flip), wrong start, backwards assignment.

options: They forgot to flip > to < — this still finds the biggest
exercises.explanation: The one change that makes min out of max is flipping > to <. Leaving > means it still finds the maximum.

exercises.prompt: What is the one-character fix for the code above?
exercises.explanation: Flip the sign: 'if n < best'. That single change turns the max loop into a min loop.

exercises.prompt: A learner starts the smallest at a big number: best = 9999. Why can that be risky?
options: If a value is bigger than 9999, or you guess wrong, best may never match a real value — start at nums[0] to be safe
exercises.explanation: Guessing a 'big enough' start is fragile. Starting at the first real value always works and mirrors the max start.

options: The assignment is backwards — it should be best = n
exercises.explanation: 'n = best' loses the smaller value. Save the winner INTO best. This is the exact same bug you watched for in max.

exercises.prompt: Leaving 'best = n' un-indented (outside the if) would make best end up as the LAST value, not the smallest.
exercises.explanation: Without the if guard it runs every pass, overwriting best each time. Same indentation trap as the max loop.

exercises.prompt: Someone claims 'min needs a totally different loop from max.' Are they right?
options: No — it is the same loop with > flipped to <
No — min needs no loop at all
exercises.explanation: That is the core message: min and max share one pattern. Only the comparison differs.

exercises.prompt: You run a 'smallest' loop on [-3, -1, -7] and it returns 0. What is the likely bug?
options: best was started at 0 instead of nums[0]
there is no bug — 0 is correct
exercises.explanation: 0 is not even in the list. Starting best at 0 (and perhaps a leftover > ) breaks it. Start at nums[0] and use <.

exercises.prompt: Which of these correctly find the SMALLEST? (pick all)
options: start best at nums[0], replace when n < best
start best at nums[0], replace when n <= best
start best at nums[0], replace when n > best
start best at 0, replace when n < best
exercises.explanation: First two use the flipped comparison and a safe start (< and <= land on the same min). The third finds the biggest; the fourth breaks on negatives.

exercises.prompt: You test your min on [1, 2, 3] (already rising) and it returns 1. Why is that a weak test?
options: The smallest is conveniently first; test lists where it sits in the middle or is negative
exercises.explanation: A rising list puts the min first, hiding bugs. Put the smallest in the middle, and try negatives, to really check.

exercises.prompt: A quick way to tell a min loop from a max loop at a glance is to look at the comparison sign.
exercises.explanation: < means smallest, > means biggest. Reading the sign tells you which the loop finds.
